analysis.one_liner: Caps the size of the nation's biggest banks and requires them to hold far more capital.
analysis.headline: The Senate Banking Committee held a hearing but never voted; the bill died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would force the largest bank holding companies to shrink and to finance themselves with more of their own money instead of debt. It caps any bank holding company at 10% of all U.S. deposits and requires violators to sell deposits to other firms. It requires firms with $50 billion or more in assets to hold tangible common equity worth at least 10% of their assets, counting off-balance-sheet positions. It also caps nondeposit liabilities at roughly 2% of GDP for bank holding companies and 3% of GDP for large nonbank financial companies such as insurers.
analysis.who_benefits: Depositors and taxpayers, because a banking system made of smaller, better-capitalized banks is less likely to need a taxpayer-funded rescue when one fails; and smaller banks, which would gain deposits and compete on a more level field.

how_it_helps.text: Caps any bank holding company at 10% of total U.S. insured deposits and directs the Federal Reserve to force violators to sell or transfer deposits to unaffiliated firms, effectively requiring the very largest banks to divest branches and customers.

Requires bank holding companies with $50 billion or more in assets, and large nonbank financial companies, to hold tangible common equity of at least 10% of average total consolidated assets, counting off-balance-sheet positions, so big firms absorb more of their own losses instead of creditors and taxpayers.

Caps nondeposit liabilities at 2% of U.S. GDP for bank holding companies and 3% of GDP for nonbank financial companies supervised by the Federal Reserve, limiting how large a nonbank financial firm can grow relative to the whole economy.
Requires the Federal Reserve to present a corrective-action plan to the banking committees within 60 days when a firm violates the limits, with periodic reports and testimony until the firm complies.

analysis.who_pays: Shareholders and executives of the largest bank holding companies and big nonbank financial firms, who would see profits from debt-financed growth cut and would have to sell off deposits, assets, or businesses to comply within one to three years.
analysis.who_pays_short: Megabank shareholders and big financial firms

drawbacks.text: Firms out of compliance at enactment would have as little as one year to sell deposits, assets, or off-balance-sheet items to reach the new limits, and rapid forced sales in a short window could disrupt credit and asset prices during the transition.

Supporters of large banks argued at the time that hard size caps could push lending to less-regulated lenders outside the banking system and raise costs for large corporate borrowers who rely on a few big banks for credit; the bill contains no provision addressing that shift.

The bill leaves significant discretion to the Federal Reserve, including separate liability limits for insurance-affiliated firms and exemptions from deposit-liability calculations for firms with international operations, which could soften the caps in practice.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core benefit — making the largest banks fund themselves with more equity so failures cost shareholders rather than taxpayers — is real, and counting off-balance-sheet positions closes a loophole that let risk stay invisible on paper. The main cost is the transition: a one-year compliance deadline for the deposit, liability, and leverage limits could force hurried asset sales, and shifting some lending outside the regulated banking system is a genuine trade-off. On balance, the design addresses the specific weakness exposed by the 2008 crisis — a handful of institutions so large and leveraged that their failure threatened the whole economy — with limits that are simple to enforce.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee, which held a hearing but never brought it to a vote, and it died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on May 9, 2012, together with Sen. Tom Harkin.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
The committee held hearings, printed as S.Hrg. 112-679, but took no further action on the bill.
It had 3 cosponsors: 2 Democrats and 1 Independent.
No markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the bill expired at the end of the 112th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest bank holding companies are better off: no firm had to shrink, sell deposits, or hold the 10% equity cushion, and the status quo of concentrated banking continued for the rest of the 112th Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The largest banks and their shareholders

for.name: Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which would cap bank size and raise capital requirements for the largest firms.

for.name: Tom Harkin
for.what_they_did: Joined in introducing the bill alongside Sen. Brown.

against.name: Tim Johnson
against.role: Chair, Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or vote; the committee's only action after referral was holding and printing a hearing.

against.name: The largest U.S. bank holding companies
against.role: Banks above the bill's size and capital thresholds
against.what_they_did: Opposed proposals to cap bank size and force divestitures, and lobbied against break-up bills in the Senate.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship stayed with progressive Democrats and one Independent, and no Republican support is recorded, while the Democratic-led Banking Committee took no action, so the bill never drew the broad coalition needed for a vote.

industries.industry: Large bank holding companies ($50B+ in assets)
industries.note: The bill forces any bank holding company over the 10% deposit share to divest deposits and requires the biggest firms to hold twice as much equity capital as they did, directly cutting profits from debt-financed growth. Their interest in the bill ran against depositors and taxpayers, who bear the cost when a heavily levered giant fails.

Deposits sold off by oversized banks would flow to smaller competitors, and a cap on giant institutions levels the competitive field that size advantages and too-big-to-fail funding perks currently tilt.

industries.industry: Large nonbank financial companies and insurance-affiliated firms
industries.note: Supervised nonbank financial companies face a 3%-of-GDP liability cap and the same 10% equity requirement, but the Federal Reserve may set separate, potentially lighter limits for firms primarily in insurance and may exclude foreign deposits from the calculation.
